Public stress-testing methods, compared out-of-sample

Each target is forecast with methods published by the IMF, the Federal Reserve and the New York Fed, and with three benchmarks. Every method is re-estimated at every origin from 2012Q4 on (every quarter), using only data up to that origin, and forecasts 1–12 quarters ahead with the macro values that actually happened. Errors are on the level: percent of the actual level for balances and income, units (percentage points) for rates.

Methods are ranked by the metric chosen in ranking.metric. The tail metrics (RMSE, 90th percentile, the average of the worst errors, the largest error) punish a method that is right on average but sometimes deviates a lot; every metric is computed at each horizon and averaged over horizons 1–12.

The methods

IMF: Bayesian model averaging with sign constraints

At every origin the candidate drivers (series with an expected sign in the target's sign file) are screened on their partial correlation with the target; the best 10 with the right sign are kept (at most 2 per theme, no near-duplicates), each at its best lag 0-2. Every combination of 0 to 3 of them is estimated as yi,t = ai + ρ yi,t-1 + Σ bk xk,t-lag with bank fixed effects. Equations whose long-run multipliers bk/(1−ρ) have the wrong sign are discarded. The forecast is the average of the remaining equations weighted by exp(−BIC/2), which is Bayesian model averaging with equal prior odds. Nothing is selected: every admissible equation contributes.

Guerrieri & Welch (Fed): forecast combination

One equation per macro variable: yt on yt-1 and lags 1-4 of that variable (bank effects in a panel). The 10 variables most correlated with the target are used (signs are not imposed, as in the paper). The forecast is the equal-weighted average of the equations.

NY Fed CLASS-style: one fixed, simple equation

One small equation per target with drivers chosen on economic grounds (set in config.yaml under class_drivers), estimated on the panel, and kept identical at every origin. A transparent challenger.

Federal Reserve: income = rate × balance

For an income target, each method forecasts the parts (rates and balances) and the income is rebuilt from them with the same formula, instead of forecasting the dollar amount itself. Shown as “method (rate x balance)”.

Accounting identities

When targets are linked by an identity (total loans = mortgages + commercial loans, say) and all of them are forecast in the run, their forecasts are made to add up: either every target moves a little, the least certain forecasts the most (weighted least squares reconciliation, Hyndman et al.), or one target takes the whole gap. Shown as “method (identities)”, next to the unadjusted forecasts. With only some of the targets in the run, or identities_on: false, the identity is ignored.

Asymmetric effects (IMF BMA with rises and falls)

The same Bayesian model averaging, but each driver may also enter with separate slopes for its rises and its falls (max(x,0) and min(x,0)), for example unemployment hurting more when it rises than it helps when it falls. The asymmetric form costs one more parameter in the BIC, so it only takes weight when the data support it; both slopes must have the expected sign. Stays linear in each regime, so it extrapolates into severe scenarios.

Monotone piecewise-linear effects

The core drivers of the BMA (inclusion probability of at least 0.5, Barbieri & Berger's median probability model) enter as piecewise-linear curves with knots at the terciles of their history. The curve may bend, but every piece must slope in the expected direction (estimated by bounded least squares), and the end pieces continue in a straight line beyond the data, so severe scenarios still have an effect.

Linear model + monotone boosted trees

The BMA's weighted-average linear equation, plus shallow gradient-boosted trees fitted to its residuals and constrained to be monotone in each driver's expected direction. Trees are flat outside the range of their training data, so beyond history only the linear part moves the forecast: the trees add curvature where there is evidence, the linear part extrapolates. Nonlinearity helps most in uncertain and stressed periods (Goulet Coulombe et al. 2022), but with about 100 quarters it must earn its place out-of-sample.

Direct forecasts (smooth local projections)

Instead of one quarterly equation iterated forward, one equation per horizon h for the cumulative change over h quarters, on the current change and each driver's cumulative change over the same h quarters of the scenario (a local projection, Jorda 2005). All horizons are estimated together with a penalty on the second differences of the coefficients across h (a P-spline with a knot at every horizon), so the paths are smooth, as in the smooth local projections of Barnichon & Brownlees (2019); coefficients are bounded to their expected sign. Iterated forecasts are more efficient when the model is right; direct ones are more robust when it is misspecified (Marcellino, Stock & Watson 2006; Chevillon 2007), at the cost of more variance at long horizons (Li, Plagborg-Moller & Wolf 2024). direct uses the BMA's core drivers, direct_class the CLASS-style drivers.

Benchmarks

AR(1) with bank effects; drift (the bank's average change); random walk (no change).

Conformal bands

The 80% and 95% bands come from the out-of-sample errors of the same method at the same horizon (finite-sample conformal quantiles of log errors for balances, of differences for rates). The coverage columns check them honestly: at each origin the band is built only from errors already known at that origin, then compared with what happened.

Reading the results

  • The test is conditional on the macro path that happened. That is the right test for scenario models, but real forecasts also carry the error of the macro forecast itself.
  • The coverage columns should be close to 80% and 95%. They are computed in real time: early bands are built from the errors of the calm years only, and then meet the shocks of 2020 and 2022, so coverage below the nominal level is the usual result and an honest warning. The scenario bands are wider, because they use every out-of-sample error, shocks included.
  • The example data are simulated. On them the true drivers are known (see the data notes of the main project), so the BMA inclusion probabilities can be checked against the truth; on real data they are evidence, not proof.
  • All equations are in changes. A target that is pulled back towards a level (a rate that tracks a bond yield, say) is better served by an error-correction term, which none of these published methods uses by default.
